No Booker Prize winner's book was published in 1950, because the prize began in 1969. The search turned up two related points:

- **Hypothetical list:** A London Review Bookshop post imagined who would have won if the prize had existed from 1900. Its list names Doris Lessing's The Grass is Singing for 1950 (1950 The Grass is Singing, Doris Lessing). This is a retrospective exercise, not a real award.
- **Real winner with a 1950 book:** P.H. Newby, who won the first Booker Prize, also published a 1950 novel, The Young May Moon (1950), per FantasticFiction. The source lists it as a novel but does not say whether it was ever shortlisted, and the Booker went to his 1969 book, Something to Answer For.

Also relevant: the prize originally covered books from the previous year, and from 1971 onwards, it was awarded to books published in the same year as the prize. So a 1950 publication could never have been a regular winner under the rules.

The search turned up the 1950 Pulitzer winners, but one framing issue first: Pulitzer prizes are awarded in a given year for books published the year before. So the 1950 awards went to books from 1949, not 1950. That's from my own knowledge, and the sources don't state it directly for these titles.

**1950 Pulitzer winners found in the results:**
- **Fiction:** A.B. Guthrie Jr. won for *The Way West*. He was a novelist, screenwriter, historian, and literary historian, and also spent 22 years as a reporter and editor at the Lexington Leader.
- **Poetry:** Gwendolyn Brooks won for *Annie Allen*. Per one source, she was the first African-American writer to win a Pulitzer Prize in any of the letters categories.
- **Biography:** Samuel Flagg Bemis won for *John Quincy Adams and the Foundations of American Foreign Policy* (listed under the 1950 entries of the Biography Pulitzer).
- **Drama:** The results list *South Pacific* only as a finalist, not a winner.
- **Journalism (Public Service):** The prize went to the Chicago Daily News and St. Louis Post-Dispatch.

The results didn't include a complete list of 1950 winners across all categories, so the Pulitzer.org 1950 page (https://www.pulitzer.org/prize-winners-by-year/1950) is the best place to verify and fill gaps.

Conrad Richter's novel *The Town* was first published on April 24, 1950, by Alfred A. Knopf. Publisher: Alfred A. Knopf. Publication date: 1950. The book, his eighth, was published on April 24, 1950.

It is the third book of the Awakening Land trilogy, set on the Ohio frontier. The other two are The Trees (1940) and The Fields (1946). It won the 1951 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. The Town was awarded the Pulitzer Prize in 1951.

Richter's birthplace is most often given as Pine Grove, Pennsylvania. He was born on October 13, 1890, in Pine Grove, Pennsylvania, a town named by his great-grandfather, a tavern keeper. One source, manoflabook.com, instead says he was born in Tremont, PA, which conflicts with the other sources. Pine Grove is the better-supported answer.

The novel was first serialized in Cosmopolitan and then published in book form in 1950. Sources differ on the British release date.

- **Serialization:** It ran in five parts in Cosmopolitan magazine, from February to June 1950.
- **US book edition:** Scribner's issued the American edition in September. One seller lists a first printing of 75,000 copies, published on September 7, 1950.
- **British edition:** One seller says the British edition came out three days earlier, on September 4th. A Jonathan Cape listing gives May 16, 1950, which conflicts with that date. I'd treat the May date as the less reliable of the two.
- **Commercial success:** It reached The New York Times bestseller list in 1950. It was Hemingway's only novel to top the list.
- **Title origin:** The title comes from the last words of Confederate General Thomas J. "Stonewall" Jackson.
- **Context:** Scholars describe the book as his literary comeback, written during a period of unsteady health.

The search turned up several figures, and they don't all agree.

- **Current population:** The 2020 census count most often cited is 54,583, which would make Oak Park the 26th-most populous municipality in Illinois. One mirror of Wikipedia gives this figure (It is the 26th-most populous municipality in Illinois, with a population of 54,583 as of the 2020 census.). Other sources give different numbers: 54,318 as of the 2020 census, and a 2010 figure of 51,878. The surf wiki page also lists 51,282 in its infobox.
- **Historical peak:** One source says the village reached about 64,000 around 1930 ("by 1930, the village had a population of 64,000, even larger than the current population").
- **Hemingway's birthplace:** The house is at 339 North Oak Park Avenue in Oak Park, and the Ernest Hemingway Birthplace Museum was opened to the public in 2001.
- **Population when he was born:** One travel site says the population was only around 500 when he was born. I'd treat this with caution. It conflicts with the 64,000 peak source and with the village's rapid growth after 1871, and I found no census citation for it. Hemingway was born July 21, 1899, per a genealogy source (21 July 1899).

Bottom line: Oak Park's population is roughly 54,000–55,000 based on the 2020 census, with the exact figure depending on the source. The "around 500" figure for 1899 is unverified.

Now I have all the information needed. Let me also confirm that Ernest Hemingway, MacKinlay Kantor, and Conrad Richter were all Pulitzer Prize winners.

- **Ernest Hemingway** — Won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1953 (*The Old Man and the Sea*) and published *Across the River and into the Trees* in 1950. Birthplace: Oak Park, Illinois.
- **MacKinlay Kantor** — Won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1956 (*Andersonville*) and published *Lee and Grant at Appomattox* in 1950. Birthplace: Webster City, Iowa.
- **Conrad Richter** — Won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1951 (*The Town*, published 1950). Birthplace: Pine Grove, Pennsylvania.

The retrieved evidence directly names all three authors as prize-associated and with 1950 publications. The Booker Prize did not exist in 1950 (it began in 1969), so no Booker Prize winners published in 1950 qualify under that prize's history.
